- When sentiment is high (≥0.6) and forecast shows a sharp upward move, reduce the forecast by 5–10% to avoid over-optimism.  
- When sentiment is low (≤0.3) and forecast is trending down, avoid excessive downward correction — allow slight mean reversion but don’t overshoot below 1–2% below recent low.  
- If forecast shows a spike followed by a steep drop, reduce the peak by 10–15% and smooth the decline to avoid “overshoot after spike” bias.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days of history show strong mean reversion (e.g., 2–3 consecutive days of price decline), adjust forecast to reflect slower decay, not abrupt drop.  
- If sentiment is rising (e.g., 0.4–0.7) and forecast is flat or slightly declining, add a small upward bias (2–5%) to account for sentiment-driven momentum.  
- Avoid forecasting below 50% of the 18-day moving average unless sentiment is clearly bearish and confirmed by 2+ consecutive low sentiment readings.
